aldemar.headline: The deal expires and Trump threatens the mediator — Brent takes $90
aldemar.standfirst: The 60-day memorandum that had held since June lapsed on Monday with neither side willing to extend it. Trump demanded Iran "put up the white flag of surrender", said he is "not in a hurry", and threatened to bomb Oman — the country mediating the talks — if it gets in the way. Brent took $90, WTI closed 84.50, the 30-year yield hit 5.31% (its highest since 2007) and the S&P gave up 0.45% to 7,750.48 with the VIX up 6.6%. All three of your names moved on it: BAC tagged 65.23 intraday and closed at the session low, INTC bounced 1.0%, GOOG slipped 0.6%.

positions.title: 1 signal on BAC — read before the open (INTC quiet)

items.html: BAC — BAC tags 65.23 intraday and closes at the low of the day — the resistance in your thesis held. Monday printed a high of 65.23, clean through the 65 level you flagged, then closed 63.89 — the session low — on a day the 30-year yield hit 5.31%, its highest since June 2007. A steepener that good and the stock still could not hold above 65 is the market telling you where the supply sits. Gabriel is −0.76% on entry at −0.12R with the stop 5.8% below at 60.39; Aldemar −0.42% at −0.06R, stop 7.1% below. Nothing here is broken — the entry was a pullback trade and the level is doing exactly what a resistance level does — but a second rejection at 65 would change the character of it, and the retail earnings landing this week (Home Depot, Walmart, Target) speak directly to the consumer-credit side of the thesis.

INTC — INTC +1.0% to 103.49, recovering part of Friday's giveback. A bounce with no news attached — chips traded better while the broad tape fell, which reads as position-squaring rather than the BofA CPU thesis being re-litigated. Gabriel is −1.95% on entry at −0.21R, stop 8.3% below; Aldemar −2.19% at −0.09R, his 81.10 stop 27.6% below. Its own put wall at 105 is still overhead: Monday's high of 105.97 poked through and failed to hold, so that level is now resistance rather than support until it closes back above.

positions.note: Signal changes the thesis, the levels or the size — earnings, a regulator with teeth, M&A, a ruling with a revenue line attached. Everything else is filed as noise on purpose; a real signal survives skepticism.

themes.right: MoU expired · no extension · Hormuz shut
themes.title: The negotiation window closed and nobody asked for more time

items.html: The 60-day memorandum of understanding expired Monday; neither side moved to extend it. The framework that had capped the conflict since mid-June is simply gone. Both sides had accused each other of violating it for weeks, and its lapse removes the structure that oil had been pricing an extension of.

Trump threatens to bomb Oman "if it gets in the way" of reopening the strait. Oman is the mediator, a US ally, and was itself hit by Iranian drones earlier this year. Threatening the one channel both sides still use is the clearest signal yet that Washington has stopped treating a negotiated reopening as the base case.

"White flag of surrender" — and no timetable: "I'm not in a hurry". Trump also claimed direct contact with the IRGC. Iran's foreign minister Araghchi answered that Tehran has "not yet made a decision to restart negotiations" and that Hormuz "will remain Iranian". Two maximalist positions with no process left between them.

Brent takes $90; WTI closes 84.50, up 2.55%. The premium that spent last week rebuilding got its confirmation. This is the third consecutive higher close and the level that starts feeding the inflation path again rather than merely tracking headlines.

themes.note: The transmission is oil → inflation → the regime call, and Monday reversed the direction it had been running all last week. Two cooling prints had pulled CPI y/y to 3.3 against the 2.5 floor — clearing by 0.8 — and pushed September to a hold; crude at these levels pushes that gate back open and keeps Policy tightening alive rather than expiring. The 30-year at 5.31% is the same message from the bond market: energy and deficits, not policy. For the book this cuts both ways — a steeper curve is the BAC thesis, while higher input costs and a 6.6% jump in the VIX are the tax on everything else. The next thing that would change the read is any signal that talks restart; there is currently no scheduled channel for that to happen through.

world.title: Yields at 2007 highs, oil at $90, and a market that finally noticed

items.html: The 30-year hits 5.31%, its highest since June 2007; the 10-year climbs to 4.72%. The long end keeps selling off through cooler inflation prints, which makes this a fiscal-and-energy verdict rather than a policy one. It is a direct headwind for long-duration equity and the cleanest support for owning a lender.

S&P −0.45% to 7,750.48, Nasdaq −0.30%, Dow −0.46%; VIX +6.6% to 15.19. The first session in three weeks where volatility rose meaningfully. Still only 0.6% off Thursday's record, so this is repricing risk rather than exiting it — but the VIX had been under 15 for a fortnight, and that complacency just ended.

Crude's third straight higher close as the Hormuz deadline passes without a deal. Energy was the one place to be. With the strait shut and no negotiating framework left, the supply question no longer has a scheduled resolution date attached to it.

Home Depot, Walmart and Target report this week. They land straight after a −0.6% retail sales print and a sentiment reading of 51. Guidance is the read-through on whether the consumer is genuinely cracking — which matters more to the BAC credit thesis than any rate move this week.

weekly.headline: The week the market started auditing the AI bill — and the war stopped pretending
weekly.standfirst: Five sessions, a third straight weekly gain, and a record close on Thursday: the S&P added 0.36% to 7,785.76 while the VIX fell to 14.25. Underneath that calm, two things changed. Investors began pricing how AI infrastructure is financed rather than what it might earn — Alphabet on Tuesday, Broadcom and Applied Materials on Friday — while the CPU side of the same trade got re-rated upward. And the war moved from rhetoric to enforcement: a US helicopter disabled a tanker running the blockade, Hormuz traffic sank to three-month lows, and the interim deal now expires on Tuesday.

Two inflation prints cooled, one consumer cracked, and the AI trade split in half

TECHThe AI capex audit begins: GOOG −3.6% Tuesday on a $25bn bond deal, AVGO −6% Friday on a $370bn financing question. Alphabet's quarterly capex hit $44.9bn with free cash flow negative for the first time; Broadcom was marked down on how a lease-and-debt structure gets funded. The market spent this week deciding that the cost of the build belongs in the valuation.TradingKey · Yahoo Finance · 11–14 Aug
SEMISBofA lifts the 2030 CPU market from $170bn to $210bn — INTC ran 6.3% Thursday before fading 2.0% Friday. Vivek Arya's argument is that AI moving from training to inference resets the GPU-to-CPU ratio toward 1:1. It is the bull case for both INTC positions, and Friday showed it will not travel in a straight line.Motley Fool · BofA · 13 Aug
DATACPI cooled Wednesday, PPI cooled Thursday to 4.7% from 5.5%, then retail sales fell 0.6% Friday. Three prints that moved September from a coin flip to a hold. The tone changed midweek: the first two were disinflation, the third was demand weakening — the same direction with a very different meaning for earnings.BLS · AP · 12–14 Aug
RATESThe 30-year auction clears at 5.216% — the highest in a quarter century. The long end refused to follow the cooler prints down, which is a fiscal and energy verdict rather than a policy one. It is the single cleanest reason to be long a bank here.Yahoo Finance · 14 Aug
NOISEFiled and ignored: Pixel 11 previews, an Alphabet 11-year retrospective, a $107.66 Intel target already overtaken. A week's worth of commentary that arrived after the moves it described. None of it touched a thesis, a level or a size.various · 10–14 Aug

The through-line is that this market has stopped paying for AI ambition and started pricing AI arithmetic — who is writing the cheques versus who is cashing them. You now hold one of each: Alphabet writing them, Intel cashing them.

From rhetoric to Hellfire missiles in five sessions

STRIKEA US Navy helicopter disables the M/V Vela Nova with two Hellfire missiles in the Gulf of Oman. The first commercial vessel fired on since the ceasefire, and the moment the blockade stopped being a declaration. Engine room and steering gear, deliberately disabling rather than sinking.12 Aug
SHIPPINGHormuz traffic falls to near three-month lows as both sides claim control. Trump says the strait is open under US control; Iran says nothing passes without its permission. The traffic data settles it — whoever is right, the tankers are not sailing.13 Aug
MILITARYHegseth: the blockade can hold "indefinitely"; a relief carrier group sails Friday. Words backed by a rotation schedule. The market's hope that enforcement fades on its own was removed this week.13–14 Aug
OILWTI rose 4.7% on the week to 81.84 while equities made a record. Energy finished as the week's best sector. Crude is carrying the war risk that the equity indices are not.10–14 Aug

The week's arc runs from talks-are-close on Monday to a missile strike on Tuesday to annexation talk on Friday. Nothing was signed, and the June interim deal now expires on Tuesday 18 August with the blockade live and both sides demanding compensation from the other.
